newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asia Metals-Doubts grow on Tokyo aluminium futures.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals-Doubts grow on Tokyo aluminium futures.

text.p: Japan's spot metal markets slumbered in the past week, digesting a heavy influx of imports early this month, while doubts grew over Tokyo's new aluminium futures contract as turnover tumbled, traders said on Friday.

"The turnover (in Tokyo aluminium futures) is so low, we don't want to get involved," said one spot trader at a major trading house. "We also have to see first how much physical metal changes hands when the nearby October contract expires."

On the Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM), where aluminium futures were launched on April 7, daily turnover dived to about 4,000 lots, one-fifth of the 20,000 lots the exchange had expected. Volume hit a low of 2,517 on Monday.

Traders said it was unfortunate that the contract set sail at the same time that the London Metal Exchange (LME) was hit by heavy fund selling and the yen weakened to 127.16 yen to the dollar, its lowest since August 1992.
Some traders said the TOCOM contract's fortunes should turn around when LME prices end their current consolidation phase and start ticking upward again.
But not everyone was optimistic, particularly given the speculative nature of TOCOM, where the main players are individual investors rather than suppliers or users.

"Something has to happen. Otherwise, the TOCOM futures will suffer the same fate as COMEX (aluminium futures), which failed to spur any interest," said another physical trader at a major trading house.

He said he would use TOCOM prices instead of LME prices only if such a need arose. Yet neither big end-users nor trading houses saw much merit in TOCOM's main selling point -- that contracts are traded in smaller lots of 10 tonnes instead of the LME's 25.

One trader said the lack of interest in TOCOM was evident in the decision by Japan's trade houses to place jurisdiction over TOCOM aluminium futures trading in their precious metal sections rather than their light metal sections, as precious metal traders were already familiar with the machinations of TOCOM, where gold and platinum futures are also traded.
In the physical aluminium market trade remained slack, with end-users gauging the direction of the country's economy after an increase in the sales tax at the start of this month.

Many traders said premiums were steady at around $85 per tonne, but others said they were under pressure after U.S. benchmark premiums slipped below six cents a lb from a high of about seven cents in March, hit when flooding disrupted shipping operations.
One trader said he saw deals at a premium of only $75.
The copper market was quiet apart from continued small-lot buying from China, traders said.
"We've seen the yen decline. (Yen-based) copper prices are still too high for Japanese users," said one trader at a major trading house.

Traders saw little activity in the zinc market, which they expected would remain quiet for the near future following heavy imports under the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) scheme at the beginning of this month.
